article.plain_text:
In February, OpenAI told the industry to stop reporting SWE-bench Verified and to use Scale AI's SWE-Bench Pro instead. In September, Scale shipped a repaired version of Pro, and on 16 October it published the paper behind it. On the repaired version, Claude Code with Opus 5 resolves 99.4% of the tasks. Codex with GPT-6-Astra resolves 96.9%. Kimi-K3, running in a minimal open-source scaffold, resolves 97.5%. A year ago, the best model solved 23% of the original set.
Read quickly, that says AI agents can now do almost any real software engineering task you hand them. I wanted to know what exactly they were handed. So I opened all 731 tasks of the original release and all 642 of the repaired one, and compared what the agent is told with what the hidden tests check.
The result: the issue text names 10% of the new functions, classes and fields that the hidden tests call. The full prompt names 81%. The difference comes from two fields Scale added to every task, "requirements" and "interface", which describe the solution: the names, the signatures, often the exact behaviour. After the October repair the figure is 88%.
That is not a scandal, and this piece is not an exposé. Scale designed it that way for a sound reason, and the repair made the benchmark fairer, not easier to game. But it changes what a 99% means. It is the score of an agent that implements a specification written by a person. The specification was the hard part, and the benchmark supplies it.
This piece has the method, the numbers task by task, the repair in Scale's own figures, the scores of all eleven systems, and my reading of what it means for anyone who funds or builds with these agents. The code to reproduce every number is linked at the end.
From 23% to 99% in thirteen months
The 23% and the 99% are not the same test: the first is the original 731 tasks, the second the repaired 642. The speed is part of the story anyway, so here it is in order, from the primary sources.
21 September 2025. Scale releases SWE-Bench Pro: 1,865 tasks from 41 repositories, of which 731 are public. It was built against contamination, using copyleft repositories and private code, with multi-file tasks that take a professional hours. The best public scores at launch: GPT-5 at 23.3% and Claude Opus 4.1 at 22.7%.
 
23 February 2026. OpenAI publishes why it no longer evaluates SWE-bench Verified. In a 27.6% slice of the dataset that models often failed, at least 59.4% of the problems had tests that reject correct solutions. And every frontier model it tested could reproduce the original human fix, the gold patch, from memory. Its recommendation: report SWE-Bench Pro.
 
Scale welcomed it the next day as recognition of "the new standard for frontier coding evals".
 
Meanwhile, December 2025 to April 2026. Vendor launch posts climb on Pro: GPT-5.2 at 55.6%, GPT-5.4 at 57.7%, GPT-5.5 at 58.6%. Anthropic's Opus 4.7 post adds a footnote that its memorization screens flag a subset of problems in the SWE-bench evals, Pro included. OpenAI's GPT-5.5 post repeats the warning.
26 May 2026. Datacurve publishes an audit of 789 Pro trials. In 32% of them, its re-grading disagreed with Pro's verdict: 24.0% were correct solutions marked as failures, 8.5% wrong ones marked as passes.
8 July 2026. OpenAI publishes Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations. Its human reviewers found 249 broken tasks out of 731 (34.1%), its automated pipeline 200 (27.4%), and it estimates about 30% are broken. It notes that frontier models went from 23.3% to 80.3% on the public split in eight months, and it retracts its recommendation to adopt Pro.
 
1 September 2026. Epoch AI rates SWE-Bench Pro "Flawed" on its benchmarking hub.
September and October 2026. Two independent repairs arrive: OpenCompass's SWE-Bench Pro Verified (8 September) and Scale's own V2 (shipped 22 September, paper on 16 October). On V2, the top system resolves 638 of 642 tasks.
 
One detail in that sequence is worth stopping on. Scale's own leaderboard for v1, which runs models in a standard scaffold, topped out at 61.5%. The 80.3% OpenAI cites does not appear there; it matches a vendor-reported run on the vendor's own agent. Same tasks, nearly twenty points apart. Before we even get to the tasks, a coding score is partly a score of the harness around the model.
What a task looks like
Take one task at random, from navidrome, an open-source music server written in Go. The agent gets three pieces of text.
The issue. Its title is "[Bug]: GetNowPlaying endpoint only shows the last play". It describes a symptom a user would notice: the "now playing" list shows one entry when several people are listening, because players are identified by user name, client and a loosely defined type field, so entries overwrite each other. That is a normal bug report. To fix it, you have to work out how players should be identified instead and where that logic lives.
The requirements. Nine bullet points, written by Scale's annotators. The first one: the Player struct must expose a UserAgent string field, with JSON tag userAgent, instead of the old Type field. The second: the PlayerRepository interface must define a method FindMatch(userName, client, typ string) (*Player, error). The rest say what Register must accept, what it must return, when it updates LastSeen, and what it must persist.
The interface. A short block: name FindMatch, type exported interface method, path model/player.go, inputs, outputs, and one line on what it does.
The hidden test, TestCore, checks exactly those names and that behaviour. The issue never mentions FindMatch or UserAgent. The requirements and the interface name both, with the file to put them in.
I don't think that is wrong. A test that calls FindMatch can't pass if the agent, quite reasonably, calls the method FindByIdentity. Without the names, a correct fix fails. But notice what the agent no longer has to do: decide that the fix is a new identity model, choose its shape, and pick where it goes. A person did that, and wrote it down.
The question is how typical this is. So I counted.
Fix a bug, or build something new?
The first thing to measure is what kind of work the tasks are. A fix to existing code rarely needs a new name: the tests call functions that already exist. A feature does: the tests call something the agent must create.
I counted, for each task, the functions, classes, methods, types and fields that the reference solution defines and that the hidden tests call. I kept only genuinely new names: not on a removed line of the same patch, at least five characters long, and not generic words like result or value.
 
In SWE-bench Verified, the 500-task benchmark from 2024, 19 tasks (4%) have hidden tests that call a name the agent must create. Those are mostly bug fixes inside code that already exists.
In SWE-Bench Pro, 353 of 731 tasks (48%) do. Half of the "hardest" coding benchmark is building something new to a shape the tests already expect. That is closer to real work, which is one of the reasons Pro was built. It is also why Pro needs a way to tell the agent what shape to build.
What the agent is told before it starts
Now the main count. For those 353 tasks there are 818 new names that the hidden tests call. How many of them appear in the text the agent receives?
 

 
The issue text, the part that looks like a real bug report, names one in ten. The two added fields bring it to four in five. In three of every four tasks that need a new name, the agent is told every one the tests will call.
The same holds for exact strings. When a hidden test asserts that an error message reads a certain way, the message is in the prompt more than half the time in v1, and 70% of the time in V2. I counted only strings with a space in them, so these are messages and labels, not file paths or field names.
For comparison, the same count on SWE-bench Verified gives 68%. But it rests on 28 names in 19 tasks, because Verified rarely asks for new names at all, and its issues are real GitHub issues, so when a name appears it is because the user who reported the bug wrote it.
Why Scale did it, and why it is defensible
Scale explained the two fields in the original paper. The requirements were added "to resolve any potential ambiguity issues". The interface exists because "models may misname classes or function names", and the paper calls it important for "mitigating false negatives for unit test verification".
OpenAI's February post gives the same problem from the other side. Its example of a "narrow test" in SWE-bench Verified is a task whose tests import a function the prompt never mentions: a correct fix with a different name fails. Pro's interface field is built to prevent exactly that. And even with it, "overly strict tests" that enforce details the prompt doesn't state is the first category in OpenAI's July audit of Pro.
Hidden tests are a blunt instrument. They call specific names with specific arguments and compare specific outputs. An issue written by a user never says any of that. Without some description of the expected interface, many correct solutions would fail for naming reasons alone, and the benchmark would measure the agent's luck at guessing a test author's vocabulary.
So the requirements and the interface are a fairness fix. The cost is that the benchmark stops measuring one of the hardest parts of the job: turning a symptom into a design. My count puts a number on how much of that part is supplied.
The repair: 480 of 731 tasks
The October release went further. Scale's team audited every task and published the result in a paper, SWE-Bench Pro V2 (arXiv 2610.24206, 16 October 2026).
 
They repaired 391 tasks and discarded 89: 480 of 731, or 66%. The largest group, 247 tasks, had a defect in the verifier or the environment: the grading setup, not the agent, decided the score. One example from the paper: the old verifier applied the hidden test patch over the agent's working tree, so a correct patch that also touched a test fixture could not be graded. That alone cost two of the systems 44 runs on v1.
The second group, 141 tasks, had an unstated test requirement: the tests demanded behaviour the task never mentioned. Scale fixed most of them by stating it. That is why the requirements grew. In my count, the median task has 7 requirement bullets in V2, up from 6, and the requirements are longer than the issue in 71% of V2 tasks, up from 54%. The paper's own illustration: of 27 tasks whose instructions were repaired, 18 had been failed by every configuration on v1, and 15 are now solved by every frontier system.
The repair also closed the obvious shortcut. During the agent run, the sandbox can reach only the model endpoint, and the images no longer contain the fixing commit in their git history. The paper is candid about why. Before network access was cut, one frontier model copied the reference solution verbatim from GitHub on 351 of the tasks it solved; only 237 of those still held up once GitHub was blocked. With the network open, 32 of 642 Opus 5 trajectories contacted code hosts. The 99.4% was measured with the network closed. The audit took 23 contracted engineers 404 hours.
That matters, because a second, independent repair of the same 731 tasks found the same weakness. SWE-Bench Pro Verified, by Zheng et al., published under OpenCompass (arXiv 2609.08149, September 2026), blocked code hosts, hid test files and refined 102 tasks. For GLM-5.2, blocking the shortcuts turned 186 passes into failures, and the score fell from 78.8% to 59.5%. I joined the two datasets task by task. Of the 102 tasks OpenCompass rewrote, Scale's V2 drops 17 and keeps 85. Scale does not publish which of its kept tasks it repaired, so I can't say how far the two audits agree beyond that.
So the honest summary is not "the benchmark was gamed". It is: the old scores were a mix of agents finding the answer online, graders failing correct work, and tests demanding things nobody said. The repair removed all three. What is left is clean. And what is left, an agent implementing a stated specification under a fair grader, is nearly solved.
The scores, all eleven systems
These are Scale's numbers from the V2 paper, Table 2, each system in the scaffold it was run in. "Hard" is a 51-task subset Scale selected as the most difficult.
 
Two things stand out. First, the spread on the full set is twelve points from first to last, including small and open models. The benchmark no longer separates the frontier. Second, the Hard subset still does: 98% at the top, 53% at the bottom.
I checked whether the Hard tasks are hard because they are less specified. They are not. In the Hard subset, 91% of the new names the tests call are in the prompt, against 87% in the rest. Hard tasks are just as fully described; they are harder to implement. I come back to this below, because it is the strongest argument against my own reading.
My reading: three jobs, and the benchmark measures one
Here is how I think about it, as someone who builds with these agents every day.
Software work is three jobs. Deciding what to build: turning a symptom, a customer complaint or a business need into a design, with names, boundaries and behaviour. Building it: writing the code that meets that design inside a real codebase. Checking it: knowing whether what was built is right.
SWE-Bench Pro, by design, gives the agent most of the first job (81% of the names, in my count, and much of the behaviour), measures the second, and does the third with hidden tests the agent cannot see. A 99% says the second job is done: given a precise specification in a real repository, frontier agents implement it almost every time.
That is a big result and it deserves to be said plainly. Two years ago agents could not reliably do the second job either. Now they can, across Go, Python and JavaScript, in codebases as large as Ansible, Teleport and OpenLibrary.
What the score does not say is that agents can do the first job. Nothing in the benchmark tests it, because the hidden tests need the names fixed in advance.
For investors, that changes how to read a coding score in a pitch or a launch post. "95% on SWE-Bench Pro" now means "implements a well-written spec". It does not mean "replaces the engineer who writes the spec", and it no longer separates one frontier lab from another. If the value of coding agents comes down to implementation, the scarce part of software moves to the two jobs around it: writing specifications precise enough to hand over, and checking the result. That is where I would look for the next durable products, and for the next benchmark that matters.
For developers, the result is a recipe, and a useful one. The benchmark is a large, well-controlled experiment in what makes agents succeed. Write the task the way Scale writes it, and agents deliver.
The recipe: write it like a SWE-Bench Pro task
This is the shape of a Scale task, reduced to a template. Every field is something the hidden tests depended on.
 
Three practical points come out of the numbers.
Name the things your tests will call. Most failures this kind of spec prevents are not intelligence failures, they are naming failures. If your test calls FindMatch, say FindMatch.
Give exact strings when they matter. If a message will be compared, quote it. V2 does this in 70% of tasks that test a message.
Keep the design for yourself, and write it down. The agent was not asked to design FindMatch. Someone decided that players are identified by user, client and user agent. That decision is still the job, and it is the part to review hardest.
Where I could be wrong
A name is not the code. Knowing that the method is FindMatch(userName, client, typ string) still leaves the implementation: the query, the persistence, the edge cases. The Hard subset proves that a full specification does not make a task easy: it is just as specified as the rest, and the weakest systems solve barely half of it.
My measure is a count, not an understanding. It matches names with regular expressions. It misses names introduced in ways the patterns don't catch, and it counts a name as given when it appears anywhere in the prompt, even in passing. I checked a sample by hand and the matches were genuine, but the 81% is an estimate with some noise in both directions.
I cannot show that specified tasks are solved more often. Scale publishes aggregate scores, not results per task. So I can show what the agent is told, and I can show the top score, but not the link between the two task by task. If per-task results are released, that is the first test I would run.
The fields exist for a good reason. Without them, correct solutions would fail on naming. Any benchmark with hidden tests faces this trade-off. Mine is a reading of the trade-off Scale chose, not a claim that it chose wrong.
Verified is not a clean comparison. It is a different set of repositories, all Python, built from real GitHub issues. The 4% versus 48% contrast is about the kind of task each benchmark asks for, not about which one is better.
Method, and how to reproduce it
Data: the three public datasets on Hugging Face, ScaleAI/SWE-bench_Pro (configs v1 and default, the V2), opencompass/SWEBench-Pro-Verified, and princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified, downloaded on 25 October 2026.
For each task, the script collects the names the reference patch defines on its added lines, keeps those the hidden test patch calls, and drops any name that also appears on a removed line (a rename or rewrite, not a new name), any name under five characters, dunder methods, and a short list of generic words. It then checks whether each name appears, as a whole word, in the issue text and in the full prompt. The core of it:
 
Expected strings are string literals of 8 to 80 characters, containing a space, that the fix adds and the hidden tests assert. The per-task table, the summary and the scripts are in the research repository: github.com/con-golias/workings.
Reruns take under a minute on a laptop.

Altman and Huang sold you 99.9%. ARC Prize's own table says 62.7%.

Same model, GPT-6 Astra, same benchmark, ARC-AGI-3. On ARC Prize's standard neutral harness it scores 62.7% at max effort, at $26,098 a run. On OpenAI's provider adapter harness it scores 98.6% at max and 99.9% at high effort. Hold the model and the effort fixed, change only the harness, and 36 to 45 points move.

What changes is what the model gets to carry between requests. The standard harness lets it keep only the notes it chooses to preserve. The adapter preserves an opaque reasoning state and compacts long conversations, so it reuses prior work instead of solving from scratch.

To be fair to OpenAI, the adapter isn't cheating. On the 167 pairs both harnesses solved, adapter runs were about 3.66x faster and used 49% fewer tokens. That's a real engineering result. But a model-plus-scaffolding score presented as a model score can't rank labs against each other. Huang cited the 99.9% in September and declared AGI had arrived. That declaration was built on the adapter number.

The practical takeaway is boring and useful: never quote a headline benchmark score without asking which harness ran it. Right now the harness is half the score.

The strongest competitive advantage in the AI era is neither superior hardware nor superior software, but the ability to optimize hardware and software together.

The market is still taking a rather crude approach, lumping a wide range of companies together under a single concept. Traditional cloud computing is software-driven, and software development follows the principle of abstraction because differences in underlying hardware performance are relatively small. But AI computing clusters, particularly massive clusters comprising tens or even hundreds of thousands of GPUs, have shattered that abstraction.

For a cloud service provider to gain a genuine competitive advantage in the AI era, building a closed loop of deep hardware control and precise software coordination is one path to establishing substantial differentiation. If a cloud provider lacks sufficient control over its hardware, its software capabilities may not translate into actual performance, or it may be unable to receive the feedback it needs. Therefore, the optimal approach should involve:

Bottom-up feedback: hardware informing software. Physical infrastructure feeds real-time information about power-distribution bottlenecks, network congestion, and node-failure warnings into the cloud-native software orchestration layer.

Top-down control: software adjusting hardware behavior. Based on the priorities of training and inference workloads, software dynamically adjusts power allocation across the cluster, partitions computing resources, and coordinates data storage with GPU scheduling.

This also includes capabilities that require close hardware-software collaboration, such as hardware-level multi-tenancy, network and switch isolation, and physical and logical GPU slicing technologies.

These technical requirements are precisely why new companies have an opportunity to compete on equal footing with established cloud giants in this industry. Software strength alone is not enough, and neither is the hardware strength of traditional cloud providers. In this new era, companies will have a chance to emerge as winners only if they excel at optimizing both hardware and software in coordination.

The AI industry is still in its early stages, and AI infrastructure is still taking shape. The concept of the neocloud remains extremely vague. Does bare metal have the advantage? Does software have the advantage? Neither, on its own. Of course, the market is enormous, and for a considerable period, there will be room for many players to survive. But to become truly competitive in this industry, a company must be strong in both software and hardware coordination.

Infrastructure is undergoing enormous changes. Companies deeply involved in building this new infrastructure will gain advantages in physical facilities. The software capabilities developed on top of that foundation will gradually take shape, purpose-built for the new hardware infrastructure. As a result, they should perform exceptionally well in coordinating increasingly complex systems. I have already seen this trend emerging at the recent GTC conference in Berlin, and it has also been validated by several software capabilities NVIDIA recently developed in collaboration with IREN.

This year, the market has viewed NBIS as having this potential and awarded it a high valuation. NBIS wants to build an integrated, self-contained system, placing particular emphasis on its full-stack software capabilities. However, it cannot match IREN in the scale and depth of its infrastructure deployment. This gap will become increasingly apparent over time, particularly when it comes to individual gigawatt-scale sites. Leasing can make it relatively easy to secure numerous smaller sites quickly, but sites exceeding 300 MW are much harder to secure. Gigawatt-scale sites are effectively out of reach for a leasing-based model.

IREN is building a flagship AI factory for NVIDIA's DSX system. There will be many things that only IREN is positioned to undertake, such as developing individual gigawatt-scale sites, clusters of multiple gigawatt-scale sites located in close proximity, and sophisticated interactions with the power grid. IREN and NVIDIA could well develop multiple reference configurations at different megawatt scales for the market to choose from, ranging from small sites to hyperscale facilities. Throughout this process, IREN is participating extensively in the standardization of AI infrastructure, giving it a strong first-mover advantage in physical infrastructure.

On this foundation, the cloud technology team IREN is assembling will play a critical role, developing software optimized to interact and coordinate with the new AI infrastructure. Throughout this process, its vertically integrated model will prove enormously valuable.

Competition has never been about winning at a single point; it is a massive exercise in system-wide coordination. Even Elon Musk appears underprepared in this regard. His approach of scrambling to pile computing capacity onto gas turbines as quickly as possible may resemble a peacock spreading its feathers: everyone sees the impressive display at the front, but no one notices what is going on behind it. In my view, regardless of whether he can actually pull it off, even if he succeeds, the economics of this approach will likely be very poor. Tesla was built around an uncompromising focus on cost efficiency, but when it comes to AI, that philosophy seems to have turned into spending whatever it takes. I am not convinced by this approach.

As my research has deepened recently, I have come to understand more and more of the decisions IREN has made over the past year. IREN is a deeply involved builder of the AI infrastructure that is now taking shape. By collaborating with leading companies in the AI industry, it is positioning itself as a leader in physical infrastructure, while building a powerful software ecosystem for optimization and coordination on top of that foundation.

Nokia and Nvidia’s Extreme Co-Design: From Two Separate Visions to One Drawing Board

To better understand how this alliance came about, I had to take a trip down memory lane. @PeterBr70324445  brought this to my attention. He told me that I needed to see the bigger picture and that this would be of immense value to anyone who has invested in Nokia or plans to.

To do so, I had to compare the strategic moves of both companies over the past 20 years.

While CEO @JensenHuang was building the compute side, successive CEOs at $NOK were forging the Interconnect and Edge. The result is that Nokia now finds itself at the heart of @nvidia GB300 ecosystem.

Part 1: The Simultaneous Timeline (2006–2026)

In this first part, I’ll discuss the parallel development of both companies, starting with @nokia and NVIDIA’s investments in a future that the stock markets didn’t yet understand at the time.

Phase 1 (2006–2013): Sowing Early to Be the First to Reap

NVIDIA: In 2006, Jensen Huang introduced CUDA—for those unfamiliar with it—a programming platform designed to harness the parallel computing power of a GPU for demanding general-purpose computing tasks. 

He envisioned every graphics card becoming a supercomputer. The process cost billions, was slow, and analysts complained about margins for years. But the stubborn visionary Jensen Huang was already looking much further ahead as early as 2011! He spoke openly about expanding CUDA to mobile platforms and even the physical world.

NOKIA: At the same time, the mobile phone segment was taking a massive hit due to the rise of the smartphone. It was decided via Nokia Siemens Networks to focus on high-capacity mobile data infrastructure instead (4G/LTE).

The parallel: Both companies share the same long-term philosophy—building the fundamental architecture for a data-driven world…

Phase 2 (2014–2019): Suri’s Vision of the Programmable World

NOKIA: Rajeev Suri became Nokia’s new CEO in 2014. He decided to permanently shut down the phone division and presented his vision of a future where the physical world would be automated and connected through smart networks: The Programmable World. To make this a reality, Suri made his masterstroke in 2016: the acquisition of Alcatel-Lucent and, shortly thereafter, network analytics specialist Diepfield. With these moves, he secured the crown jewel: high-capacity IP routing (7750 SR), optical transport lines (1830 series), and Bell Labs.

NVIDIA: In 2016, Jensen Huang launched the first DGX AI supercomputer, followed by the acquisition of Mellanox in 2019. He realized that for thousands of GPUs to work together, the network is the bottleneck.

The Convergence: The visions of both CEOs begin to align. Huang focuses on internal connectivity, while Suri builds a network connecting data centers to the outside world.

Phase 3 (2020–2024): Building the Optical AI Stack

NVIDIA: The AI market explodes following the launch of the H100 and B200. Data centers are bursting at the seams and scaling from megawatts to gigawatts. The distances between GPUs become too great for copper cables, making optical data transmission and power consumption the new bottlenecks for AI scaling.

NOKIA: In 2020, Pekka Lundmark becomes the new CEO, and under his leadership, Nokia launches SR Linux (an open-source operating system for data center switches). He is also heavily investing in tactical 5G for defense. But it wasn’t until 2024 that he took the decisive step with the acquisition of Infinera. This gave Nokia ownership of ICE-D coherent optical technology and its own indium phosphide chip manufacturing capabilities.

The Convergence: To solve the problem of Nvidia’s gigawatt data centers, Nokia now has all the necessary building blocks:

- Alcatel routing
- SR Linux
- Deepfield
- Infinera optical

Phase 4 (2025–2026): Time to Reap the Rewards

NOKIA: In April 2025, after completing the Infinera acquisition, Justin Hotard took over from Lundmark. As the former head of Intel’s Data Center & AI Group and former HPC leader at HPE. It’s clear that Nokia brought him on to capitalize on the AI infrastructure built by Suri and Lundmark.

NVIDIA: Having already acquired a $1B equity stake in Nokia, Jensen introduces the term that sums up this twenty-year journey during the launch of the GB300 NVL72 and the 1GW Omniverse DSX AI Factory blueprint: “Extreme Co-Design.”

Part 2: Together at the Drawing Board—The 1 GW Blueprint

To find concrete evidence of the joint blueprint, we only need to look at the Zankore project—a joint venture between Nokia, NVIDIA, Ooredoo Group, and Indosat that was launched in August 2026. Zankore is building a 1GW NVIDIA DSX AI Factory in Southeast Asia.

The architecture: The facility runs on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems combined with DSX MaxEPS/MaxLPS dynamic power management, which increases usable computing capacity per megawatt by up to 40%.

And now for Nokia’s role: The ONLY AI-native network partner within this reference design. Nokia provides THE ENTIRE PHYSICAL AND OPTICAL INTERCONNECT INFRASTRUCTURE, both in-house and with the external telecom network!

Led by Zankore CEO Ulf Ewaldsson (former CTO of rival Ericsson), this project serves as the standard blueprint for future 1GW AI Factories worldwide. This is the result of extreme co-design: Nokia and Nvidia design their hardware and network architecture together from the drawing board as a single system.

Part 3: The Technical Architecture Within the Data Center

Okay, this part is very technical, but necessary to understand Nokia’s value in this system.

1. Coherent Optical Efficiency (ICE-D + 1830 GX):

The challenge in transmitting data from a data center to the outside world is that short-distance signals (standard light) typically need to be converted into long-distance signals. This requires additional transponders that consume a lot of power and introduce latency.

The solution Nokia offers is to precisely tune the ICE-D optical components (Infinera) to the modulation formats and spectral profiles of its 1830GX Multi-rail line systems. The powerful laser (colored light) for long-distance transmission (ICE-D chip) has been miniaturized to the size of a USB flash drive and plugs directly into the switch or router. This enables IP-over-DWDM. DWDM (Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing) is a technique in which dozens of different data streams are transmitted simultaneously over a single long-distance fiber-optic cable by assigning each its own color of light (wavelength). Data center switches now send data directly to the global fiber-optic network. This results in up to 50% less power consumption, more bandwidth at the network layer, and a faster connection.

2. Telemetry and Troubleshooting (SR Linux + Deepfield)

The problem here is that AI training models are susceptible to interruptions. During a checkpoint synchronization (interim saving of progress during training), a single faltering connection can shut down a cluster of 100,000 GPUs, which naturally leads to GPU idle time.

The solution: Nokia’s data center switches run on SR Linux. Combined with the Deepfield analytics engine, this provides real-time visibility from the individual GPU transceiver all the way to the long-haul fiber-optic cable (1830GX). If there’s a problem with a fiber-optic line kilometers away, internal switches immediately reroute traffic. This way, the GPU cluster doesn’t experience a timeout.

3. Zero-touch optical automation (1830GX + 7750 SR)

The problem: Manual configuration of large-scale networks is time-consuming when scaling up data centers.

The solution: The 7750 SR router platform and the 1830 GX optical system share a single central control plane. Once a router card is plugged in, the 1830 GX automatically detects it, sets the correct wavelengths, and optimizes power without human intervention. Deployment time drops from days to minutes.

Part 4: Closed Ecosystem & Mobile Integration

Total Stack Enclosure: Nvidia and Nokia jointly deliver pre-validated, software-defined computing pods that are ready for immediate deployment. No months-long integration processes for data center administrators.

Mobile Network as an Extension (Physical AI)

By integrating Nvidia’s CUDA architecture with Nokia’s mobile 5G and 6G radios (AI-RAN), the mobile network becomes a direct extension of the data center. External applications such as autonomous robots, vehicles, and defense systems are thus directly connected to the AI-Factory.

In this post, I’ve tried to objectively demonstrate that all the pieces of the puzzle have fallen into place, that this is no longer a distant dream, and that the seed for this was planted about 20 years ago….

The paper analyzes 30K production training traces and identifies 3 bottlenecks in LLM pre-training:

1. Cross-DC checkpoint reads bottlenecked by WAN round-trip time (RTT).
→ Copy checkpoints to the evaluation datacenter in advance and prioritize urgent evaluations.
2. Slow training restarts when thousands of GPUs request the same files at once.
→ Create extra copies of frequently accessed files (based on predicted access patterns) before training starts.
3. Slow image and video processing that leaves GPUs waiting for data.
→ Use available CPUs on storage servers to prepare data before GPUs need it.

Results:
• 76.1% lower evaluation I/O time
• 40.8% faster checkpoint loading
• 63.2% fewer data-loading stalls

Takeaway: Profile the entire training pipeline, not just GPU utilization. Use workload predictability to anticipate I/O demand, replicate hotspots before training starts to ease the load and speed up reads, move preprocessing closer to storage when compute resources are available.

article.plain_text:
Elon said most of the 200+ neoclouds could dry up as debt markets shut them out.

The usual take: SpaceX will just buy the good ones cheap.
He said there's no point.
That only sounds weird if you think SpaceX is in the same business as the neoclouds. It isn't.

The consolidation is real
Pure-play GPU cloud providers took on large amounts of debt and leases to lock in scarce GPUs and power, betting AI demand would grow fast enough to cover the cost. Gartner and several industry executives now expect the majority of independent neoclouds to disappear or get absorbed within a few years. Only a handful with real scale, strong customers, and access to capital are likely to remain standing.
Musk pointing this out isn't particularly controversial. What's less obvious is why he has little interest in picking up the pieces.
Training and inference are different jobs
Frontier training wants the largest possible coherent cluster: uniform high-end GPUs, extremely high-bandwidth interconnects between them, and low latency across the whole system so a single training job can scale efficiently. These runs are large batch jobs that can last days or weeks. Once a newer, bigger, more uniform cluster is ready, companies prefer to put the next major training run there.
Inference — serving the model to users — works differently. It is continuous, scales with actual usage, and is less sensitive to perfect inter-GPU connectivity for many workloads. Older or mixed hardware can often handle it well enough. The capacity also needs to stay online and responsive rather than being locked into one giant training job.
This distinction matters for how clusters get used. An older facility can still be valuable for inference, fine-tuning, or secondary training even after it is no longer the preferred place for the next frontier training run.
SpaceX already has the capacity it wants — on its own terms
After merging with xAI, SpaceX built Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 at unusual speed. Colossus 1 was large enough that xAI could move its main training work to the newer cluster and still have substantial capacity left. That is the capacity Anthropic took (roughly 300 MW / 220,000+ GPUs at Colossus 1, with additional capacity across the sites), paying about $1.25 billion a month.
Utilization on Colossus 1 had been low relative to its size. There were also practical limits: mixed GPU generations that created bottlenecks, and network latency issues when trying to treat multiple campuses as one coherent training cluster. Those problems made Colossus 1 less ideal for xAI's own frontier training runs, but still useful for inference and other workloads. Renting it out was a better outcome than leaving it underused.
Older clusters don't suddenly become worthless. They simply stop being the preferred place for the next largest training job once a bigger, more uniform cluster is ready. The older capacity shifts toward inference, fine-tuning, secondary training, or external rental.
Why buying a neocloud doesn't solve the problem
SpaceX's constraint is not a shortage of third-party GPU hours. It is building and operating the exact clusters it wants — at the power density, interconnect quality, and operational control required for frontier training — under its own timeline.
A neocloud typically offers leased or managed capacity on someone else's infrastructure, with different power arrangements, different networking, and different operational constraints. Acquiring one would give SpaceX more GPUs and more contracts, but not the next Colossus built the way it wants. It would still need to construct or heavily rework the physical plant to match its requirements.
That is why the "buy the distressed neoclouds" idea is largely irrelevant to what SpaceX is doing. The company is already acting as a large-scale compute landlord (Anthropic, Google, and others) while simultaneously expanding its own clusters. It prefers short or flexible rental terms so it can reclaim capacity if internal needs grow. The strategy is to own and operate the infrastructure directly rather than depend on external providers for the workloads that matter most.
The actual bottleneck
The broader market remains short of readily available inference capacity, which is why SpaceX itself has reportedly struggled to rent inference compute from the major clouds to free up its own clusters for training. Power, interconnects, and the ability to stand up large coherent clusters quickly are the binding constraints, not a lack of companies willing to sell GPU hours.
Musk's comment about neoclouds and debt markets is about the fragility of the pure-play rental model under current financing conditions. His lack of interest in acquiring them is about a different priority: controlling the next generation of capacity on SpaceX's own terms instead of inheriting someone else's.
Agree or push back — curious where you land.

A Chinese AI lab just revealed numbers that could change how you think about the AI business.

DeepSeek has open-sourced its inference engine, and the economics behind running AI are getting REALLY interesting.

But here's the question: if AI is this cheap to run, why are OpenAI and Anthropic still operating at a loss?

Let me explain.

First, you need to understand three things.

GPUs are AI chips manufactured by companies like NVIDIA and AMD. Multiple GPUs are connected and housed together in a rack. Multiple racks combine to form a cluster.

DeepSeek has a cluster with 2,400 GPUs.

Now, every time you ask ChatGPT or another cloud-based AI service a question, your prompt and the response are processed as tokens. That's what much of the AI industry charges for.

Here's where it gets interesting.

DeepSeek recently revealed real-world inference numbers. According to the reported figures, a single cluster serves 155 trillion tokens per day.

And a single GPU generates almost $38 in revenue per hour.

These are off-peak figures. During peak hours, that revenue reportedly nearly doubles.

And according to researcher Yichun, even if you rent NVIDIA's latest B300 chip, the economics can still be surprisingly interesting.

But here's the catch: revenue is not profit.

Running AI isn't just about paying for GPUs. These companies also have to cover infrastructure, electricity, networking, data centres, model training, research and development, engineering teams, and the cost of serving millions of users.

And then there's the subscription problem.

A $20 ChatGPT subscription doesn't mean every user costs OpenAI the same amount. Some users barely touch the service, while others run intensive workloads all day. Heavy users can consume significantly more computing resources.

So even if inference becomes cheaper, that doesn't automatically mean the entire business becomes profitable.

But DeepSeek's approach raises a much bigger question.

If inference costs keep falling and open-source models keep getting better, will companies like OpenAI and Anthropic be able to justify their subscription prices?

Or will AI eventually become so cheap to run that today's pricing models stop making sense?

The real AI race isn't just about who builds the smartest model. It's about who can serve intelligence at the lowest cost and turn that into a sustainable business.

@elonmusk  this weekend: the 200+ neoclouds face "guppy-level death and consolidation." Also Musk: "SpaceX is not buying any neoclouds. Pointless."

Fair. He doesn't need their buildings. He needs the chips that would have gone to them.

We said on Oct 20 the rent was fine and the market was pricing the cost of money. Musk makes the same point, with more fish. Two things he leaves out.

1) The chips

Musk endorsed a list of what limits a supercomputer build: land, permits, grid, transformers, fuel, even lathes. GPUs aren't named.

SpaceX ($SPCX) calls 10 GW of new capacity in 2027 "highly certain," mostly on Nvidia's Vera Rubin. SemiAnalysis puts all new data-center capacity outside China in 2027 at 51.2 GW and says the next bottleneck is chips and HBM. That's one buyer taking about a fifth.

Nvidia has lined up $170bn+ in investments and commitments to help customers finance their builds. That's how you keep a lot of buyers alive, not how you let one of them take a fifth of the build.

On its call, SpaceX said it wanted to rent outside inference capacity to free its own GPUs for training, and couldn't find any.

2) The lease

SpaceX rents short, at spot. Anthropic or SpaceX can walk on 90 days' notice. The split is about half rented, half in-house, flexing to 60/40, and the contracts let SpaceX move capacity between tenants and its own training. A 440k Vera Rubin cluster for Grok is due by mid-2027. At today's rents, payback is under a year.

So tenants pay down the GPUs while compute is scarce. When it isn't, the GPUs go to Grok.

CoreWeave ($CRWV) and IREN wrote the opposite contract: average backlog terms above ~5 years, per Bernstein, and IREN keeps nothing back for spot. A neocloud GPU has one job: rent. A SpaceX GPU has two.

Our call: if rents cool, the first sign won't show up in CoreWeave's or IREN's numbers. It'll be SpaceX moving capacity from tenants to Grok.

When one landlord predicts the rest will go under, read his lease.

今天下午五点四十五，央行发了一条公告，编号〔2026〕第12号。名字很长：债市非银大额赎回互换便利，英文缩写四个字母，BNSF。两百来字。我读了三遍，第一遍一个字没记住。

说白了是这么回事。往后债市要是真出了大乱子，银行理财和公募基金可以从央行借一样东西。借的是央行票据，押到市场上去换钱，把自家被赎回的产品买回来一点。救急用的，平时不发。

我盯着这条公告看了半天，觉得它其实认了一件事。债市里最危险的东西，坏资产还真排不上号。最危险的是同一分钟。

先说件特别小的事。四个人合租，一个卫生间。早上七点半，四个人都要洗脸刷牙。卫生间没变小，人没多一个，谁的需求也没多一分。可那二十分钟，它就是不够用。到了九点，一整天没人排队。

债市这件事，是这个卫生间的放大版。理财和基金拿着别人的钱去买债。债要到期才还本，可投资人的钱，随时能取。这个错位平时不出事，因为不是所有人同一天来取。

出事那天是这么转的。净值跌了，有人来赎。管理人手里现金不够，只能卖债。卖得多了，债价往下走。债价一跌，净值更难看。更多人跑来赎。一圈一圈，越转越快。

这圈里有坏人吗？我找了一圈，没找到。想保住本金的人没错，被迫卖债的人没错，看见抛压就往下压价的买家也没错。每个人都在做对的事，合起来就塌了。所以这次出手，管的不是人，是时间。

具体怎么管？《人民银行法》写着，央行不能直接给非银机构放贷款。这堵墙它没翻，绕了个弯：借你央行票据。票据不是现金，票据是市场上都认的抵押品。你拿它去借钱，借多少、什么价，还是市场说了算。给钱是替你扛，给票据是你自己去借。

还有一句我格外留意。公告写：参与机构应持续满足金融市场审慎管理要求。翻过来是——平时就不稳健的，出事的时候没资格来借。工具救的是市场，不是机构。这话不是客气，是防着有人提前算好：反正出了事有人兜。

TL;DR
On October 26 the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) created a facility that can supply funding to bank wealth-management subsidiaries and mutual fund managers if heavy redemptions force them to sell bonds.
It can be used only in a system-wide stress event and against high-grade collateral. Officials say it is meant to stop a sell-off from spreading and to avoid any expectation that the central bank will cover firms’ losses.
The PBOC also plans to make the overnight repo rate its main policy rate and to phase out its old benchmark deposit and lending rates.
The new facility
The PBOC calls it the Bond Market NBFI Swap Facility (BNSF), with NBFI standing for non-bank financial institutions. Eligible firms are bank wealth-management subsidiaries and mutual fund managers that the central bank considers systemically important, along with their parent banks or brokerages.
In a stress event, an eligible firm borrows central bank bills from the PBOC and uses them as collateral in the repo market to raise cash. It uses the cash to buy eligible bonds, or shares in its own funds, from products that are facing redemptions, and pledges those assets to the PBOC. Because the PBOC lends securities, the operation is a swap. China’s central bank law bars direct loans to non-bank institutions without State Council approval, which analysts cite as the reason for the design. The cash comes from other lenders in the repo market, so the operation does not add to base money or to the PBOC’s balance sheet.
 
 
The facility is for emergencies only. It applies when asset managers as a group face a liquidity squeeze and redemptions and bond sales are reinforcing each other. Firms must post high-grade collateral and meet prudential requirements for as long as they use it. Governor Pan Gongsheng, who announced the plan at the Financial Street Forum on October 19, said the conditions are there to avoid distorting market prices and to avoid any expectation that the central bank will cover losses. The size of the facility, its fees and its haircuts have not been published.
Why the PBOC wants it
Low deposit rates have pushed household savings into wealth-management products and funds, and much of that money is invested in bonds. Bank wealth-management products held 33.29 trillion yuan at the end of 2025 and mutual funds 37.71 trillion yuan. Wealth-management assets had reached 34.13 trillion yuan by mid-October.
Banks can borrow from the PBOC through repos, medium-term loans and the standing lending facility. Asset managers had no comparable access, so in a crisis the central bank could only reach them through banks. Banks tend to cut back on lending under stress, and liquidity added through them can stay in the banking system. Analysts point to the fourth quarter of 2022 as the case the facility is designed for. Bond yields rose quickly, wealth-management products lost value, investors redeemed, managers sold bonds and yields rose further.
The bond market is calm at the moment. The 10-year government bond yield was about 1.62% on October 21. In mid-October, 1.92% of wealth-management products were valued below their starting price. One brokerage says redemption pressure has typically built once that share passes 5%.
The design copies a facility the PBOC set up in October 2024 to support the stock market, which let securities firms, funds and insurers swap their holdings for government bonds and central bank bills. That facility did not cover wealth-management subsidiaries, and the new one applies the same approach to bonds.
How analysts read it
Guo Lei, chief economist at GF Securities, says sending liquidity straight to non-banks should work better than relying on banks, where it can accumulate without reaching the firms under pressure. Tan Yiming, an analyst at Tianfeng Securities, expects the facility to lower the risk of an extreme sell-off spiral. He also warns that faster movement of money among non-banks could add to volatility, and that leverage and maturity mismatches at these firms remain a risk. Another analyst argues that the facility's main effect is on expectations, whether or not it is ever used.
A new policy rate
The facility is one part of a wider overhaul Pan described on October 19. The PBOC plans to move its main open-market operations from a seven-day term to overnight, which would make the overnight repo rate its main policy rate. The PBOC has said it will choose the timing. The overnight interbank repo rate (DR001) is already the rate it targets in practice. Since June the PBOC's interest-rate corridor has run 20 basis points either side of the seven-day rate. After the switch, the policy rate, the corridor and the target rate would all be overnight rates.
Companies with strong finances will be able to choose either the overnight repo rate or the loan prime rate (LPR) as the benchmark for floating-rate loans. The LPR will remain the benchmark for small businesses and households. The PBOC will also phase out its old benchmark deposit and lending rates, and open its standing lending facility, now used mainly by city and rural banks, to foreign-owned banks and the large national banks.

The U.S. Treasury General Account (TGA) is already a widely watched liquidity indicator in financial markets.

But the latest numbers are worth a closer look.

As of October 22, the TGA balance stood at approximately $962 billion.

Now, consider the Treasury's borrowing estimates released back in July:

• Projected TGA peak at the end of October: ~$1.05 trillion
• Projected year-end balance: ~$850 billion
That's a potential decline of roughly $111.8 billion from the October 22 balance to the projected year-end level.

Of course, that doesn't mean $111.8 billion will automatically flow into financial markets. The actual trajectory depends on Treasury issuance, tax receipts, and government spending.

But there's another factor I'm paying even closer attention to: the Fed's Overnight Reverse Repo Facility (ON RRP).

As of October 23, ON RRP usage was just around $200 million.

In the past, when Treasury issuance absorbed cash from the financial system, funds moving out of the ON RRP facility could help cushion the impact on bank reserves.

Today, that buffer has been largely depleted.

This creates two potential phases for liquidity conditions:

If the TGA continues to rise through the end of October, it could put additional pressure on bank reserves.

If Treasury spending subsequently exceeds cash inflows from debt issuance and other sources, causing the TGA to decline, it could help replenish reserves.

The key is how bank reserves actually respond and whether funding markets show signs of stress.

Going forward, I think four indicators deserve particular attention:

• Actual TGA balances versus the Treasury's projected targets
• Net Treasury issuance and the maturity composition of debt
• Changes in bank reserve balances
• Short-term funding rates, including SOFR

Ultimately, what matters isn't simply the absolute size of the TGA.
It's the direction of change, where the money is coming from, and where it's going.
Treasury cash management has become an increasingly important part of the liquidity picture.
And it's something investors shouldn't overlook.

The Bond Market and Financial Plumbing Have Already Tightened Conditions

My view: the Fed holds rates steady on Wednesday. Long-term borrowing costs, heavy Treasury refinancing, and pressure in funding markets already make another hike dangerous.

• THE BOND MARKET HAS DONE MUCH OF THE WORK

With the 10-year yield near 5% and longer yields above 5.3%, mortgages, business loans, and investment already face high borrowing costs. The Fed does not need another hike to tighten conditions. The bond market has delivered that pressure.

• THE GOVERNMENT FACES A REFINANCING SQUEEZE

Treasury rolls hundreds of billions of dollars in debt each week. Older, cheaper debt is being replaced at much higher rates. Another hike would add pressure to short-term financing costs and an already heavy federal interest bill.

• THE LIQUIDITY CUSHION HAS SHRUNK

Bank reserves sit around $2.96 trillion, while overnight reverse repo balances are nearly exhausted. There is far less cash in that facility to absorb Treasury-related drains. That leaves bank reserves more exposed when money moves into the Treasury’s account.

The $3 trillion mark is a warning reference, rather than a fixed safety line for every bank.

• OVERNIGHT FUNDING IS ALREADY TIGHT

SOFR and effective fed funds are around 3.88%, close to the 3.90% interest paid on reserves. That narrow gap deserves attention, especially while dealers finance large Treasury inventories. It signals limited breathing room, although it does not by itself prove a funding freeze.

Oil above $100 takes spending power away from households and raises business costs. Higher rates cannot reopen shipping routes or remove a physical supply shortage. They would add another burden to an economy already absorbing expensive energy.

A hawkish hold: unchanged rates, with firm language on inflation.

Digital Asset Liquidity

USDC circulation stood at $71.99 billion on 22 October. That is a substantial settlement base for digital markets, but stablecoin depth cannot fully counter tighter dollar plumbing. Onchain transfer capacity can remain healthy while broader risk liquidity stays selective.

Regime

The current regime is tight. High long term yields, an elevated Treasury cash balance, falling reserves, and a firm dollar outweigh the support from stablecoin depth.

Outlook

A durable improvement would require reserve balances to stabilize, the Treasury cash balance to stop rising, the ten year yield to move convincingly below 5%, and the dollar to extend its retreat. Until then, rallies are more likely to reflect selective positioning than broad liquidity expansion.

Gold has been sending a message for some time now. The question is whether investors are interpreting it correctly.
The usual explanations for a rising gold price are familiar: inflation, geopolitical uncertainty, falling interest rates, a weaker dollar, or investors seeking protection from financial instability. All are legitimate influences, and several can operate simultaneously. Gold has experienced plenty of bull markets without fundamentally changing the international monetary system.
But something about the current environment deserves a closer examination. Governments are carrying enormous debt burdens, the cost of servicing that debt is consuming a growing share of public spending, and central banks have been accumulating gold at rates rarely seen in recent decades. Meanwhile, new trading and settlement infrastructure is being developed around physical bullion.
None of this establishes that a new monetary system is imminent. It does raise a more interesting possibility: Gold may be regaining monetary importance even if the dollar remains the world's dominant currency. That possibility is worth exploring without resorting to predictions of an overnight financial reset, a return to the gold standard, or a particular future gold price.
Gold Is Beginning to Tell a Different Story Relative to Stocks
One way to examine gold's changing role is to stop measuring it exclusively in dollars. When gold rises from one dollar price to another, we know it has appreciated in nominal terms. We do not necessarily know whether it has become more valuable relative to other financial assets. Comparing gold with the S&P 500 provides a different perspective.
The gold-to-S&P 500 ratio measures how much gold is worth relative to the level of the stock index. A rising ratio means gold is outperforming the index; a falling ratio means stocks are outperforming gold. It is not a comparison of total investment returns, because the index level excludes dividends, but it is useful for examining longer-term shifts in relative valuation.
 
Gold relative to the S&P 500, with a 40-month moving average. October 2026 is a partial observation. The ratio compares the gold price with the S&P 500 index level and does not include stock dividends.
The chart captures several distinct periods. Gold gained substantial ground against equities during the 2000s, particularly around the financial crisis and its aftermath. The relationship then reversed as equities enjoyed a long period of relative strength. More recently, gold has begun recovering ground.
The October 2026 reading in our working dataset is approximately 0.535, compared with a 40-month moving average near 0.516. That places the ratio modestly above its longer-term trend. It does not guarantee sustained outperformance, and the latest month is incomplete, but it provides a useful reason to watch the relationship. The more important question is what could sustain that shift. 
If gold is simply responding to temporary uncertainty, its relative strength may fade when financial conditions improve. If investors are beginning to assign greater value to an asset outside the credit system, the implications could be more durable. The chart cannot answer that question by itself. The broader monetary environment may offer some clues.
If you enjoy this type of analysis, I also write about the economy, financial and housing markets, monetary metals and miners, and the forces shaping them. You can find more of my research and subscribe to future articles on my Substack
The Debt Problem Is Becoming an Interest-Cost Problem
Government debt has been growing for decades, so pointing to a large debt figure is hardly a new argument for gold. Debt can expand for a very long time without producing an immediate currency crisis. The United States has repeatedly demonstrated that a government with deep capital markets, a large economy, and the world's principal reserve currency possesses considerable financing flexibility.
What deserves closer attention now is the cost of carrying that debt. According to the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee's October 22 fiscal update, the federal government recorded a $1.992 trillion deficit in fiscal 2026, with spending of approximately $7.396 trillion against revenues of $5.403 trillion. Net interest expense reached approximately $1.052 trillion, up from about $971 billion in fiscal 2025. Interest accounted for roughly 14.2% of federal spending.
Those figures do not mean the United States is about to default. They do mean that an increasingly large amount of federal revenue is being absorbed by obligations created in earlier years.
 
Growth in U.S. federal debt alongside the rising annual cost of servicing it. Debt outstanding and annual net interest expense are shown in separate panels because they measure different quantities.
The challenge is not merely that the government owes a great deal of money. It is that interest expense competes with other spending priorities while deficits continue adding to the amount that must be financed.
A government can respond through some combination of higher taxes, lower spending, faster economic growth, or continued borrowing. Inflation can also reduce the real value of existing nominal debt, although it introduces its own costs and can ultimately raise the interest rates investors demand. None of those choices is painless.
There is an additional complication. Higher interest rates can help restrain inflation, but they also increase borrowing costs as existing debt matures and is refinanced. Lower interest rates can relieve some financing pressure, but premature easing risks renewed inflation or a loss of confidence in monetary discipline.
This is where gold enters the discussion. Gold does not generate income, and it is not a productive business. Its appeal in this context is different: it is an asset whose supply cannot be expanded through a government budget decision or central-bank balance-sheet operation.
That does not make it immune to speculation or price declines. It does help explain why investors may value it more highly when they become uncomfortable with the long-term financial commitments of governments.
The Federal Reserve's Choices Are Getting More Complicated
It is tempting to describe the Federal Reserve's situation as a simple choice between fighting inflation and protecting the Treasury market. Reality is more complicated.
The Fed's monetary-policy responsibilities concern inflation, employment, and financial conditions, not guaranteeing the government a particular borrowing rate. It also retains substantial independence in setting policy. Still, the consequences of its decisions extend throughout the economy, including the federal government's financing costs.
If inflation remains persistent, policymakers may need to maintain restrictive conditions even when growth weakens. If economic activity deteriorates sharply, pressure to ease may increase even if inflation has not fully returned to target. Neither outcome automatically benefits gold.
Higher real interest rates can make interest-bearing assets more attractive relative to a metal that pays no yield. A severe liquidity squeeze can also force investors to sell gold alongside other assets to raise cash. Conversely, falling real rates, concerns about currency purchasing power, or declining confidence in fiscal discipline can strengthen gold's appeal. This is why I am skeptical of any argument that reduces gold's outlook to a single interest-rate forecast.
Gold is affected by rates, but it is also affected by confidence in the institutions responsible for money and credit. Those influences sometimes reinforce one another and sometimes pull in opposite directions.
 Gold compared with the yield on 10-year inflation-protected U.S. Treasury securities. Real yields offer a useful measure of gold's opportunity cost, although the relationship is neither constant nor mechanically inverse.
The chart is especially useful because it illustrates a relationship that investors frequently oversimplify. Gold can rise when real yields fall, but there are periods when both move higher. In those episodes, other influences—including official-sector demand, geopolitical risk, and changing confidence in financial assets—may be important.
A sustained rise in gold despite relatively attractive real yields would be particularly interesting. It would suggest that investors are willing to accept gold's lack of income for reasons extending beyond the usual interest-rate calculation.
Central Banks Are Voting With Their Reserves
Perhaps the strongest evidence that gold's role is evolving comes not from individual investors, but from central banks. The World Gold Council reports that central banks and other official institutions purchased a net 863 tonnes of gold in 2025, following approximately 1,092 tonnes in 2024.
Purchases slowed in 2025, which is important to acknowledge. But the total remained far above the 473-tonne annual average recorded from 2010 through 2021. This is not a one-year curiosity.
 
Annual net gold purchases by central banks and other official institutions. Purchases moderated in 2025 but remained historically elevated. Source: World Gold Council.
Central banks hold reserves for several reasons. They need liquidity, the ability to meet external obligations, and assets that can help stabilize confidence during periods of financial stress. U.S. Treasuries and other highly liquid securities remain essential components of that system.
Gold serves a different purpose. Physical bullion held directly by a central bank is not another government's debt obligation. It does not require a bond issuer to make payments, and it cannot be created through monetary policy. Those characteristics can become more attractive when governments are concerned about geopolitical exposure, sanctions risk, or excessive dependence on a single currency.
This does not mean every central bank is abandoning the dollar. Nor does it mean all official gold transactions represent a permanent strategic shift. Central banks also sell gold, adjust reserves for liquidity needs, and respond to changing economic circumstances.
The buying trend nevertheless suggests that a meaningful group of monetary authorities wants a larger allocation to an asset outside the conventional sovereign-debt system.
Poland provides one example. The World Gold Council reports that its central bank added approximately 102 tonnes in 2025, bringing its holdings to around 550 tonnes. The motivation extends beyond a short-term view of gold prices; reserve diversification and national financial security are central considerations. That is a different kind of demand from an investor buying gold because a technical chart looks favorable. It may also be more persistent.
 
The Dollar Can Remain Dominant While Gold Becomes More Important
Discussions of gold frequently become discussions of the dollar's supposed demise. I think that framing creates more confusion than clarity.
The dollar benefits from advantages that gold does not possess. It is supported by enormous Treasury and credit markets, extensive global payment infrastructure, established legal institutions, and a network of commercial relationships built over generations. International trade, borrowing, derivatives, and banking are deeply connected to dollar liquidity.
Replacing that infrastructure would be extraordinarily difficult.
Gold, meanwhile, is poorly suited to many everyday functions performed by modern currencies. Its price fluctuates, physical transfers require infrastructure, and a gold-based monetary regime would impose constraints that governments and financial institutions have shown little appetite for accepting.
But there is no requirement that gold replace the dollar to become more important.
A central bank can continue holding substantial dollar reserves while increasing its gold allocation. A financial institution can conduct transactions in dollars while using gold as collateral. Investors can remain heavily exposed to U.S. assets while deciding that some portion of their wealth should sit outside the credit system.
These developments are compatible with continued dollar dominance.
In fact, they may be more plausible than the dramatic alternatives often promoted in monetary commentary.
A gradual change in reserve composition would not produce a single historic announcement. It would unfold through allocation decisions, changes in market infrastructure, and the growing acceptance of gold as a strategic financial asset.
That kind of change is less exciting than a predicted monetary reset.
It may also be more realistic.
Gold's Infrastructure Is Changing, Too
Another development worth watching is the effort to expand gold trading, storage, and settlement capabilities outside the traditional Western financial centers.
Hong Kong provides a recent example.
On July 7, 2026, the Hong Kong government announced the trial launch of a central clearing and settlement system for gold. The initiative forms part of a broader effort to develop bullion trading infrastructure, including storage, refining, pricing, and connections with mainland China's gold market.
Hong Kong's government has also outlined plans for a formal system launch in the first quarter of 2027 and for new renminbi-denominated, physically settled gold futures contracts.
These initiatives do not establish that gold is about to replace conventional currency settlement. Their immediate purpose is to make the gold market more efficient and commercially attractive.
Still, the direction is noteworthy.
For decades, discussions of gold's monetary role have focused primarily on the metal sitting in vaults. Modern financial infrastructure introduces another question: How easily can that gold be valued, transferred, pledged, and settled within institutional markets?
An asset becomes more useful when the systems surrounding it become more sophisticated.
That does not turn bullion into money in the traditional sense. It can, however, make gold more practical as a reserve asset, a form of collateral, and a component of international financial activity.
The physical metal may remain the same. Its usefulness within the financial system can change considerably.
There Are Good Reasons to Remain Skeptical
Before concluding that gold is entering a new monetary era, it is worth considering the less dramatic explanations.
Gold has experienced major speculative advances before. Investors can become overly enthusiastic, particularly when price momentum attracts attention beyond the traditional precious-metals market. Exchange-traded funds, futures markets, and leveraged positioning can amplify both advances and corrections.
The World Gold Council reported substantial investment demand in 2025, including an 801-tonne increase in global gold ETF holdings. That is evidence of strong investor interest, but investment flows can reverse much more quickly than central-bank reserve policies.
Central-bank buying is also not a one-way process. The 2025 slowdown demonstrates that official institutions respond to prices and circumstances. Some countries may need to liquidate reserves during financial stress, while others may pause purchases after substantial appreciation.
And government debt, however troubling its trajectory, does not provide a timetable for a monetary crisis.
The United States still possesses a highly productive economy, exceptional financial-market depth, and the ability to borrow in its own currency. Those advantages should not be dismissed simply because the fiscal outlook is uncomfortable.
There is also a difference between gold becoming more valuable and gold becoming more important to the monetary system.
A speculative price surge could produce the former without the latter. To establish a lasting structural change, I would want to see continued official-sector demand, broader institutional use, and evidence that gold is gaining importance across different financial conditions—not merely during periods of fear.
That is a much higher standard than pointing to a rising price chart.
What Would Confirm a Lasting Change?
For me, the evidence worth following falls into three broad areas.
The first is gold's performance relative to other financial assets. If gold continues gaining ground against equities over an extended period, particularly outside episodes of acute market stress, that would suggest a more durable reassessment of its value.
The second is central-bank behavior. Continued reserve accumulation across a broad group of countries would be more persuasive than purchases concentrated in a handful of institutions. It would also be important to monitor sales and changes in reported holdings rather than focusing only on positive headlines.
The third is the development of financial infrastructure around gold. Expanded settlement systems, collateral arrangements, and institutional trading capabilities could gradually increase its usefulness beyond conventional investment demand.
None of these developments must occur simultaneously. Nor would any one of them prove that a monetary transformation is underway.
Taken together, however, they could establish that gold is becoming more deeply integrated into the way governments and financial institutions manage financial risk.
A Monetary Shift Does Not Require a Monetary Collapse
I have no interest in predicting that the dollar will disappear, that the United States will suddenly lose access to credit markets, or that the world will wake up one morning operating under a new gold standard.
Those predictions make for attention-grabbing headlines. They also demand far more evidence than currently exists.
What interests me is the possibility of a slower change—one in which gold assumes a larger role because confidence in government-issued liabilities becomes more conditional.
The dollar could remain the world's primary currency. U.S. Treasuries could remain the deepest reserve market. Central banks could continue operating under modern monetary frameworks.
And gold could still become more important.
That outcome would not be a contradiction. It would reflect a world in which monetary authorities and investors increasingly value diversification away from assets dependent on someone else's promise to pay.
The rise in gold prices is visible to everyone. The more consequential development may be occurring beneath the surface, through the decisions of central banks, governments, and financial institutions.
The question is not whether gold will replace the monetary system we have. It is whether the monetary system we have is gradually finding more reasons to hold gold.
That is the possibility I will be watching.

Research and source notes
U.S. fiscal figures: U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee, Monthly Fiscal Update, September 2026, released October 22, 2026. FY2026 deficit: $1.992 trillion; net interest: $1.052 trillion; total outlays: $7.396 trillion.
Central-bank purchases: World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends: Full Year 2025, published January 29, 2026. Net purchases: 1,092.4 tonnes in 2024 and 863.3 tonnes in 2025; 2010–2021 average: 473 tonnes.
Gold investment demand: World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends: Full Year 2025. Global gold ETF holdings increased by approximately 801 tonnes in 2025.
